title: SURF: Separation via Unsupervised Remixing Flow
topic: General Machine Learning->Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Learning
claim: A teacher's estimates are shuffled, re-estimated by a student, and remixed so the student learns from mixtures alone, with no clean sources.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right stages, with loss boxes below and an EMA arc above
description: A single wide left-to-right pipeline built on MNIST digit images. On the left, two input mixtures, each a pair of overlaid digits, go into blue 'Teacher' boxes with teacher emoji. Each teacher outputs two separated digit estimates. A gray 'Shuffle' block mixes the estimates across the pair. The shuffled estimates feed a large red-orange 'Student' region. There, noisy images and a circled-plus mixing symbol go into blue student boxes with graduation-cap and fire icons. The student's outputs pass through a gray 'Unshuffle' block and then green-ish 'Remix' blocks, which recreate the mixtures. A curved 'EMA' arrow runs from Student back to Teacher along the top. Two green rounded boxes at the bottom, 'ReMixIT' and 'Self-Remixing', receive arrows from the relevant stages and act as the training objectives. The red student region draws the eye first.
caption: Illustration of SURF. Given initial mixtures, a teacher model first produces source estimates. These are shuffled, then used as self-supervised examples to a student flow matching model. The student is trained to predict the estimated sources (ReMixIT) or original mixtures (Self-Remixing).
abstract: The goal of single-channel source separation is to reconstruct $K$ sources given their mixture. In supervised settings where vast amounts of clean source data are available, this challenging, ill-posed problem has been addressed successfully by generative diffusion and flow-based prior models. However, access to such clean source samples is often limited, and even when available, supervised models are vulnerable to domain shifts. To bridge this gap, we present Separation via Unsupervised Remixing Flow (SURF), an unsupervised flow matching approach for source separation that learns directly from observed mixtures. This method relies on a novel combination of state-of-the-art supervised flow matching and regression-based self-supervised techniques. At a high level, starting from a teacher model, we utilize a "remixing" step to bootstrap the learning of a student flow model from the teacher's estimates. We provide insights into the objectives optimized by this approach and draw a novel connection to the Wake-Sleep algorithm. Empirical evaluations on image and audio benchmarks demonstrate that SURF establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing unsupervised methods. See our demo page for examples. https://google.github.io/df-conformer/surf/
